title: Lakshmana's rage and restraint
hook: the loyal younger brother says out loud what everyone else is only thinking

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's argument, won. She answered every danger, rebuked Rama, and he said: come with me. Did you let someone change your mind? Today we step back into Kausalya's room, where someone has been burning. Day five hundred twenty-eight.

We've watched Rama be calm for days now. It would be easy to think everyone in the palace felt the way he did. Valmiki makes sure we don't. When Rama told his mother the news, Lakshmana was standing in the room. He'd been silent. Then, while Kausalya wept, he spoke, and what came out was the thing many readers are feeling by this point in the story. This is wrong. Somebody should stop it. Why isn't anybody stopping it?
screen: `NOT EVERYONE IS CALM.` → `LAKSHMANA, SILENT IN THE ROOM.` → `WHY ISN'T ANYBODY STOPPING IT?`

segments.voice: Lakshmana's anger has several layers, and Valmiki lets us hear all of them. First, it's about fairness. Rama has done nothing wrong. Who in the whole kingdom can name a single fault in him? To throw him out for no reason is against dharma itself. Second, it's about the king. Lakshmana says what no one else will say: the old man has been ruled by his desire for a young wife, and he isn't fit to judge. He goes further than that, saying the king, if he has become an enemy, should be restrained. Third, it's about action. I'm armed, Lakshmana tells Rama. I'm with you. If anyone in this city takes Bharata's side, I'll fight them all. Let Kausalya see it. Let the whole world see it. It's frightening, and it's also loyal. Every word of it comes from love for his brother. Lakshmana's name is often explained as one who bears good marks, and Hindu tradition holds him up as the model of a brother's devotion. That devotion, today, looks like a drawn bow. Kausalya, desperate, actually seizes on it. Listen to your brother, she tells Rama. Don't go. And this is where Rama's calm gets tested hardest. Not by Kaikeyi, who is his opponent, but by Lakshmana, who is on his side, offering him exactly what part of him might want. The rage is real, it's righteous, and it's within reach. Tomorrow, we hear Lakshmana's argument at its strongest, and what Rama does with it.
screen: `RAMA HAS DONE NOTHING WRONG.` · `THE OLD KING ISN'T FIT TO JUDGE.` · `I'M ARMED. I'M WITH YOU.` · `RAMA'S CALM, TESTED BY A FRIEND.` · then, large: `THE RAGE IS REAL, AND IT'S LOYAL.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath slow. Remember a time you were angry on someone else's behalf, at an injustice done to a friend or a family member. Let a little of that heat come back. Notice where it lives in the body: chest, hands, face. Don't push it away. On each breath out, notice the love underneath it, the care that made you angry in the first place. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Lakshmana's rage and restraint, part one: the rage. Loyal to the bone, he says Rama has done no wrong and offers to fight the whole city for him.
Your line: Lakshmana's rage and restraint. Today, if you get angry for someone, find the love underneath it before you act. Day five hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Hindu tradition honors Lakshmana as the model of a brother's devotion; storytellers often linger on his outburst in Kausalya's room because it voices what listeners feel.

pairs: offers to fight the whole city
begs Rama to listen to his brother
not fit to judge, Lakshmana says

myth: everyone in the palace accepts the exile calmly
Kausalya sides with Lakshmana at first
she begs Rama to listen to his brother and stay.
Lakshmana's anger is aimed at Rama
it all comes from love for Rama; it's aimed at the injustice.

fork.setup: you're Lakshmana. your brother has just been stripped of his kingdom for no fault. what do you do?
options: stay silent; it's not my place.
say it's wrong, and offer to fight for him.
fork.reveal: he speaks up: Rama has done no wrong, the king isn't fit to judge, and he'll fight anyone who takes Bharata's side.

original.note: Sanskrit lakṣmaṇa: marked, bearing auspicious signs; from lakṣman, a mark or sign.

trapdoor: what you thought: Lakshmana just follows Rama quietly.
what it means: he erupts in rage at the injustice, out of love.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki gives Lakshmana a fierce speech even against the king, and later tellings, such as the Ramcharitmanas, keep his anger but shape it more gently.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 21 (Lakshmana's outburst in Kausalya's rooms; Kausalya's plea)
